article_title: Supporting Science Learning and Literacy Development Together: Initial Results from a Curriculum Study in 1st Grade Classrooms
citation: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Study-developed NGSS-focused assessments of 1st grade three-dimensional learning and science vocabulary in-use
description: Because no off-the-shelf 1st grade NGSS science assessments existed, the research team developed two NGSS-focused assessments designed to be fair to both study conditions. The science learning assessment presents six multistep phenomenon- or problem-based tasks requiring students to interpret data tables, draw, make predictions, and select tools for investigations. The science-vocabulary-in-use assessment presents 10 science terms with definition evaluation and appropriate-use questions. Interrater exact agreement exceeded 90 percent with Cohen's kappa greater than 0.8 across all items.
requirements: Scorers with science education expertise, rubric-based scoring with rigorous training, and blind scoring to research condition
constraints: Overall internal consistency was 0.674 (Cronbach's alpha) for the science learning assessment and 0.845 for the science-vocabulary-in-use assessment
target_learning_goals: NGSS performance expectations for 1st grade across Earth and space science, life science, and physical science
examples: Both assessments were administered as whole-class activities in which teachers read scenarios and prompts aloud while students responded in their own booklets.
key_sources: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED638494

article_title: A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science Topics
citation: Schroeder, N. L., Ambarwati, Y. E., Zhang, Y., & Zhai, C. (2026). A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/MS-NGSS-Aligned-Benchmark
title: NGSS-aligned middle school and high school science benchmarks with a four-tier synthetic data quality gate pipeline
description: Two publicly released ground-truth benchmarks for evaluating LLM understanding of secondary science: "Our final dataset consisted of 1,078 items for middle school benchmark, and 1,150 items for the high school benchmark." Items were synthetically generated by Sonnet 4.6 Thinking, distributed across recall, conceptual understanding, and applied reasoning types and across 12 NGSS areas per level. Construction used "a four-tier data quality gate system" removing duplicates, enforcing Flesch-Kincaid reading-level ranges, and requiring a three-judge LLM panel to agree on both answers and standard alignment. Data and code are available on GitHub.
requirements: Items must pass duplicate removal, reading-level constraints, appropriateness checks, and three-judge agreement on accuracy and standard alignment before entering the benchmark.
constraints: Items were synthetically generated without human oversight; human review covered only a 240-item sample, and some scientific practices (graphics, data interpretation, mathematical representations) are underrepresented.
target_learning_goals: NGSS-aligned secondary science content knowledge across physical, life, earth/space, and engineering design areas
examples: Nine open-weight LLMs were evaluated answering every question three times under a standardized zero-shot prompt, with binary scoring for recall items and a three-point rubric for conceptual and applied items.
key_sources: Schroeder, N. L., Ambarwati, Y. E., Zhang, Y., & Zhai, C. (2026). A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/MS-NGSS-Aligned-Benchmark

article_title: Collaborative knowledge construction with generative AI: Exploring argumentative co-writing processes through n-gram and cluster analysis
citation: Teresa Luther · Kate Belcher · Joachim Kimmerle · Detmar Meurers · Ulrike Cress (2026). Collaborative knowledge construction with generative AI: Exploring argumentative co-writing processes through n-gram and cluster analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09470-1
title: N-gram uptake analysis: mapping human–AI co-writing onto knowledge telling and knowledge transforming
description: The article proposes analyzing textual uptake in AI-supported writing via recurring n-grams between ChatGPT output and the writer's final text, extending Bereiter and Scardamalia's knowledge telling/knowledge transforming distinction to human–AI interaction. The authors write that "Overlaps in n-grams can thus serve as indicators of uptake" and that high verbatim overlap reflects adoption "analogous to knowledge-telling activities" while reformulated use points toward knowledge transforming. The three clusters are interpreted as positions on a spectrum from passive uptake to increasingly active and integrative collaboration, aligned with the ICAP framework.
requirements: Requires the writer's prompts, AI responses, and final text so overlap between AI output and final text can be computed; recurring n-grams presuppose access to both documents.
constraints: The article states the study is correlational and the design does not allow conclusions about causal mechanisms; knowledge building is used only as a conceptual backdrop, not an operationalized outcome.
target_learners: Adult writers in academic and professional contexts (participants aged 18–71 writing argumentative texts)
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing and collaborative knowledge construction supported by generative AI
examples: Participants wrote a comment on alcohol prohibition in public with ChatGPT access; n-gram overlap classified them as reproducers, integrators, or reconstructors.
key_sources: Teresa Luther · Kate Belcher · Joachim Kimmerle · Detmar Meurers · Ulrike Cress (2026). Collaborative knowledge construction with generative AI: Exploring argumentative co-writing processes through n-gram and cluster analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09470-1

article_title: Developing a Theory of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity through Better Design: Where Do Behavioral Science Interventions Work Best?
citation: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: National Growth Mindset Intervention (NGMI) probability sampling plan
description: The NGMI study evaluates a brief online growth mindset intervention—two 25-minute sessions communicating that intelligence is malleable—delivered to 9th grade students. The sampling plan targets all 9th grade students in the 9,190 'regular' U.S. public high schools, with a national probability sample of 80 schools. Strata were created from school achievement (a latent variable based on GreatSchools.org and College Board data) and school minority composition, yielding five strata with a multipurpose allocation reported in Table 1.
requirements: Exclusion criteria as printed: only schools serving grades 9–12, excluding charter and magnet schools, schools serving special populations, and schools with fewer than 25 9th grade students
constraints: Outcomes are administrative records from the beginning of 10th grade (grades, test scores when available, course-taking measures), collected after the two online sessions
target_learners: 9th grade students in U.S. regular public high schools
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes including grades, test scores, and math course taking
examples: Table 1 shows population proportions of 25%, 27%, 23%, 20%, and 5% across the five strata, with a multipurpose allocation of 20, 24, 23, 14, and 19 out of n = 100
key_sources: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567217

article_title: Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill
citation: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a
title: NGSS three-dimensional framework integrating scientific and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and core ideas
description: The Next Generation Science Standards are a K-12 curriculum standard of the United States combining skills, understanding, and content. The article states it "combines aspects of skills, understanding, and content into three dimensions: scientific and engineering practice, crosscutting concept, and core idea". The study operationalises this framework in Indonesian grade 8 science learning by building lesson plans, worksheets, and assessment around one practice (developing and using models), one core idea (the human respiratory system), and one crosscutting concept (structure and function).
requirements: Teachers must plan learning that helps students be ready to pursue further education or a career, per the article's account of meeting the standard
constraints: The article notes that in Indonesia's Curriculum 2013 the skills to be cultivated are too complex and teachers find them difficult to assess, motivating the NGSS adaptation
target_learners: K-12 science students, operationalised here as grade 8 students in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Crosscutting concept of structure and function
examples: The study's Foundation Box pairs the practice 'Developing and using models' with the core idea 'Human respiratory system' and the crosscutting concept 'Structure and function'
key_sources: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a

article_title: Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill
citation: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a
title: NGSS-oriented learning tools: lesson plans, worksheets, and a developing-and-using-models observation sheet
description: A package of science learning tools developed for grade 8 human respiratory system instruction: lesson plans, student worksheets, and an observation sheet for assessing developing-and-using-models skill. The tools were validated by two expert lecturers, one science teacher, and nine students across two revision stages, and used in a quasi-experiment comparing an NGSS-oriented class with a control class using the teacher's tools. The article reports the tools "are feasible for use in learning, based on results of expert validation".
requirements: Worksheets must meet didactic conditions so they "could be used well for students at all levels of intelligence", appropriate language and clarity, and technical requirements of writing, drawing, and appearance
Lesson plans and worksheets are feasible if their average validation score is above 3.0; the skill appraisal tool if validation is in the good category at 76-85%
constraints: Validated for the human respiratory system theme in grade 8 at one Indonesian junior secondary school
examples: The experimental group used the NGSS-oriented tools while the control group used the teacher's learning tools during the February-March 2018 study
key_sources: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a

article_title: Comparison of virtual and in-person simulations for sepsis and trauma resuscitation training in Singapore: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Low Matthew Jian Wen, Chan Gene Wai Han, Li Zisheng, Koh Yiwen, Jen Chi Loong, Lee Zi Yao, Cheng Lenard Tai Win. (2024). Comparison of virtual and in-person simulations for sepsis and trauma resuscitation training in Singapore: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2024.21.33
title: Nominal-group-consensus assessment checklists stratified by Bloom taxonomy domains for sepsis and trauma resuscitation
description: The study's assessment instrument: marking checklists generated by a nominal group technique with 7 team members (5 attending emergency physicians, 2 fourth-year residents) using the 10th edition ATLS manual and 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines as references, with consensus defined a priori as 70% agreement. Items were then voted into cognitive, psychomotor, and affective domains using definitions from Bloom and Harrow: "definitions of cognitive, psychomotor, and affective domains from Bloom [5] and Harrow [10] were given to members as references." Reliability was good: "The ICC was 0.839 for checklists, indicating good interrater agreement."
requirements: Two calibrated blinded raters, standardized simulated assistant actions, scenario piloting, and a 14-minute per-scenario limit
constraints: Items were grouped as only-cognitive versus not-only-cognitive because all items were deemed to involve the cognitive domain in deciding to perform the action
target_learners: Junior doctors assessed on simulated sepsis and trauma resuscitations
target_learning_goals: Observation of resuscitation leadership performance across cognitive and non-cognitive skill domains
examples: Raters scored each item 0, half a point, or 1 point as not done, done inadequately, or done adequately and timely
key_sources: Low Matthew Jian Wen, Chan Gene Wai Han, Li Zisheng, Koh Yiwen, Jen Chi Loong, Lee Zi Yao, Cheng Lenard Tai Win. (2024). Comparison of virtual and in-person simulations for sepsis and trauma resuscitation training in Singapore: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2024.21.33
